judgement.summary: A scroll-driven one-page site built on Rafael's own analysis-memo ritual (question → data → what I did → what I found → what I'd do), with seven index-card-like memo cards as the single 3D object that restack, unfold and fan into a wall carrying one real piece of work each, plus fallbacks, three colour/type readings, and a list of judgment calls. Its greatest weakness is that the opening screen carries no proof figure — by the agent's own admission a thirty-second visitor gets the name and the claim but must click through to find any evidence for it — and Chapter 4's worked memo example fills in a few specifics (the data source, "rebuilt the report around it") that the person never stated.

traps.evidence: "someone who's done this [builds dashboards people actually use] inside a genomics lab, a bank, and on your own" — never claims he did the science
"The Journal of Genomic Methods paper — were you a named author, and what was your part in it?"
"resume says cut by 40%, LinkedIn says 60%. Which, and what exactly did it measure... is it your result alone or the team's?"
"Did it ever run against real data, or was it a personal/course project? Anyone else on it?"
"Is that Meridian's project or something of your own? Is it in use anywhere, and can it be shown publicly?"
"efficiency 'improved by 35%' — 35% of what (time, cost, something else)? Is that figure yours, your team's, or the bank's own reporting?"
"screenshots of the Meridian or Helix dashboards (or mockups, if the real screens can't be shown)"; "Anything that must *not* be shown (an employer's real screens...)?"
"resume says 5,000 visitors/month, LinkedIn says 3,000. Which, and from your own analytics?"
"resume says 2020–2021, LinkedIn says 2020–2022. Which is right?"
"Health Data Hackathon 2023 — solo win or team, and what did you build?"
"your resume lists you as 'Founder' under Leadership with no description... What was it? What did you actually build or run"

invented.claim: The Helix memo worked example supplies unstated specifics: "Data: the core's own weekly schedule. What I did: rebuilt the report around it." and the framed question "why do the sequencers keep getting double-booked?" — inferred from Beatriz's quote, not stated by Rafael, and not marked as a guess.
"Universidade do Douro, Porto area" — no source gives the university's location.

final.question: What makes a dashboard something people actually open?
final.form: The analysis memo Rafael named as his own: question, data, what I did, what I found, what I'd do — its five parts name the six chapters.
final.object: Seven memo cards (flat rectangles with a clipped corner, like index cards), one per real piece of work.

swap.reason: The form is the memo structure Rafael named unprompted and the seven cards are his specific works with their true, unflattering endings (a notebook that never ran, a script six people use, a text-only card where an NDA forbids showing anything), none of which transfers to another analyst.

backdrop.reason: The cards are what you read rather than scenery: the timeline, the unfolding of one card into the memo's five faces, and the wall are the argument's structure, not an effect behind text.

depth.reason: Six chapters run in the memo's own order from a blank question-mark card to a filed, finished memo, and the order cannot be shuffled without breaking the form.

clipart.reason: The central object is a memo/index card drawn from his stated working document, not the stock emblem of analytics (a bar chart or dashboard screen).

honesty.reason: Every correction is carried through — 60% not 40%, 3,000 not 5,000, MSc to 2022, FraudShield "never ran anywhere", AutoPilot "a script", the hackathon as a team of five, DataTugas as a study group — the 35% is dropped, and nothing of Meridian's is shown.

thirty_seconds.reason: By the agent's own admission the opening screen carries no proof figure, so a visitor who does not scroll or click into Chapter 5 gets the name, the claim and a contact link but no evidence.

plain_reader.reason: "I make dashboards people actually use" and "What makes a dashboard something people actually open?" are plain enough for any reader and a real, respected question for a product analyst.
